A crucial aspect for those entering the labor market in Grisons is understanding the difference between gross and net salary. The gross salary is subject to three distinct deductions. First, the federal direct tax (FDT) is calculated by Bern according to national income brackets. Second, the cantonal and municipal tax is applied by the Canton of Grisons and the individual municipalities of residence with their own rates. Third, mandatory social contributions (AHV/AIV/IPG 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAA/LAINF 0.7-1.5%, LPP 7-18% depending on age) are deducted directly from the gross salary. The final result is the net salary, which generally represents 65-75% of the gross, depending on total income, marital status, and canton of residence.
For this reason, it is essential to plan the budget considering the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) and the real purchasing power in the Canton of Grisons. A nominal salary may seem attractive, but if 30-35% is deducted for taxes and contributions, the net available for living is significantly lower.
### Negotiation scenarios in the private sector
When a candidate accepts a job offer in the Canton of Grisons, the negotiation concerns the annual gross salary, its composition (fixed plus variable, where applicable), holidays (minimum 4 weeks), the professional pension plan, and any benefits (health insurance, meal vouchers, use of company car, etc.). If the role is covered by a CLA, the employer is obliged to respect the salary structures and benefits of the contract, although they can offer higher salaries. If there is no CLA, the negotiation is more free, but the constraint of federal laws (maximum hours, minimum holidays, maternity, paternity) and cantonal laws (minimum wage, if set by Grisons) remains.
It is advisable to inform yourself at the Labor Office of the Canton of Grisons or at the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) at the federal level to verify the collective agreements in force in the sector of interest. The sectoral average salary (when available from official sources such as the Federal Statistical Office - FSO/BFS) provides a useful benchmark for evaluating whether the offer received is competitive.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Negotiation procedure and preliminary checks
Before signing an employment contract in the Canton of Grisons, it is crucial to verify some key aspects. First, check if the sector is covered by a collective labor agreement (CLA). If so, the salary offer must respect the minimums set by the CLA, although employers often offer higher salaries to attract talent. If there is no CLA, the salary is the result of direct negotiation but must still comply with the limits set by the Canton of Grisons (if it has set a minimum wage).
### Checklist for entering the job market
Six essential steps before accepting an offer:
**Check the sector**: contact the cantonal employment office to find out if there is a CLA in your sector. If there is, the employer must respect the minimums set by the collective agreement.
Compare offers: use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the net from the gross offered, taking into account the cantonal and municipal taxes of Grisons.
Check the pension: ask the employer what the contributions to the LPP (pension fund) are and at what rate they are paid. Robust pension provision is essential for your future income.
Check health insurance: LAMal (health insurance) is mandatory for residents in Switzerland; some employers contribute to the premium, others do not.
Record details: ensure the contract clearly specifies working hours, holidays (minimum 4 weeks), any bonuses, payment methods, and notice periods (1/2/3 months depending on seniority).
Plan your budget: with the calculated net, plan essential expenses (rent, food, transportation, health insurance) and verify that the salary covers your cost of living in the Canton of Grisons.
### Where to find official information
In the Canton of Grisons, the cantonal employment office (dependent on the Department of Economy of Grisons) provides data on the labor market, median salaries, current CLAs, and cantonal regulations. At the federal level, the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) manages employment and salary statistics by canton; the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) regularly publishes surveys on salaries and employment by sector and level of education. These official sources are free and reliable.
### Next steps
If you are considering a job offer in the Canton of Grisons, the first concrete step is to use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to understand your actual net income. Then contact the cantonal employment office to verify the collective agreements applicable to your sector. With this information, you can negotiate consciously and plan your budget based on the real available income.

item.title: Opening a business in Graubünden: legal forms and costs
item.description: Practical guide on how to start a business in the Canton of Graubünden: legal forms, trade register, minimum capital, registration fees and federal insurance obligations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Four legal forms: Public limited company (SA), Limited liability company (Sagl), Sole proprietorship, Simple partnership - The commercial register is managed by the cantons, not by the Confederation - Federal insurance obligations: LAMal, LAINF, AVS/AI/IPG and LPP for employees
## Key facts - **What**: Choosing the legal form and registering with the cantonal commercial register - Where: Canton of Graubünden (competent cantonal administration) - Who: Entrepreneur, employer, partners - Tax structure: 3 levels (federal, cantonal, municipal) - Registration deadline: Within 2 weeks from the actual start of the activity
### Choosing the legal form Starting a business in the Canton of Graubünden means first choosing a legal form. The main options in Switzerland are four: the Public limited company (SA), the Limited liability company (Sagl), the Sole proprietorship, and the Simple partnership. Each form has different initial capital requirements and registration obligations in the commercial register, which is managed at the cantonal level. The SA and Sagl require the deposit of initial capital with a Swiss bank. The Sole proprietorship can be started without a prescribed minimum capital if the entrepreneur operates in their own name. The Simple partnership is a form of collaboration between several people without rigid registration formalities. Each form has different implications in terms of taxation and legal liability. SAs have limited liability to the capital contributed; Sagls have limited liability; the Sole proprietorship involves unlimited personal liability; the Simple partnership has joint and several liability among partners.
### Registering with the commercial register The commercial register is managed at the cantonal level. There is no single federal register: each canton manages its own register, where companies operating in the territory must register. In the case of Graubünden, registration takes place with the competent cantonal office and involves the obligation to provide identifying data of the company, the legal form, the capital contributed, the partners, and the address of the operational headquarters. The data registered in the register is public and consultable. Registration must generally take place within 2 weeks from the actual start of the activity. Registration costs vary from canton to canton and sometimes even by municipality, as municipalities can add local administrative taxes.
### Federal insurance obligations Once the business is opened with employees, federal insurance obligations arise. All employees in Switzerland must have health insurance (LAMal), which is mandatory and must be taken out within 3 months of the start of employment. For employees, the employer must register the company with the federal pension institutions. The old-age and disability insurance (AVS/AI/IPG) requires contributions of 5.3% from the employer and 5.3% from the employee on the gross salary. If the salary exceeds the coordination threshold (approximately CHF 21,330 in 2026), registration with a LPP pension fund (second pillar) is mandatory, with contributions varying according to the employee's age. The accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) requires percentages of 0.7–1.5% of the gross salary depending on the sector of activity. Consult the [guide to corporate pensions](nav:pension) to calculate the impact of contributions. ### Tax implications of the legal form
The choice of legal form has a direct impact on the tax structure. In Switzerland, the tax system has three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. The legal form determines whether the company pays federal direct tax (FDT) as a separate entity or whether the income is attributed directly to the partners for personal taxation.
For SA and Sagl, the company is an autonomous taxable entity and pays federal FDT as an entity. The cantonal administrations (in the case of Graubünden, the cantonal administration) collect the cantonal tax based on the profit. Municipalities collect a municipal tax by applying a multiplier on the cantonal tax determined locally.
For the sole proprietorship and simple partnership, the income is attributed to the owner/partners, who declare it in their personal tax return at the federal, cantonal, and municipal levels.
### Recurring costs: registration, management, payments
In addition to the initial registration costs with the commercial register, every company incurs recurring costs. These include maintenance fees for the register (which vary by canton), costs for changes to registered data, and especially insurance and pension costs for employees.
The contributions paid by the employer include: - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% of gross salary (total with 5.3% of the employee = 10.6%) - LAINF/LAA (accidents): 0.7–1.5% of gross salary depending on the sector - LPP (second pillar): variable percentage based on age (7% for 25-34 years, 10% for 35-44 years, 15% for 45-54 years, 18% for 55+ until the reference age), calculated on the coordinated salary - LAMal (health insurance): the employer does not pay mandatory contributions, but the employee must take it out within 3 months
You can use the [federal and cantonal tax calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the actual tax burden based on the assumed income and the chosen legal form.
### Opening procedure: essential steps
Opening a business in Graubünden follows a standard procedure in all Swiss cantons, albeit with minor administrative variations:
1. Choice of legal form and drafting of constitutive acts if necessary (mandatory for SA and Sagl, not for sole proprietorship) 2. Opening a bank account with a Swiss bank 3. Deposit of the initial capital with the bank (CHF 20,000 for Sagl, CHF 100,000 for SA, or a different amount according to the statute) 4. Registration with the commercial register at the competent cantonal office of Graubünden 5. Registration with the Federal Customs Administration (FCA) to obtain the FDT and VAT number if revenues exceed the minimum threshold 6. Registration with the cantonal AVS/AI fund 7. Conclusion of insurance contracts for employees (LAMal, LAINF, LPP if applicable) 8. Notification to the municipalities where the company operates, possibly for local business taxes
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Operational Checklist and Critical Deadlines
Once you have decided to start a business, it is important to meet administrative deadlines. Registration with the commercial register must generally be done within 2 weeks of the actual start of the business. If the business has employees, the LAMal must be concluded within 3 months of hiring the first employee. Registration with the AVS fund must be done before the first contribution payment. If the company exceeds the revenue threshold for VAT obligation (CHF 100,000), registration with the AFC must be done within 30 days of exceeding the threshold.
### Required Documents for Registration
To register with the commercial register of the Canton of Grisons, you must provide: - Specific registration form of the canton (available at the commercial register office) - Copy of a valid identity document (passport, ID card, residence permit if foreign) - Notarial deed for SA and Sagl with authenticated signature - Bank deposit certificate for the initial capital paid (SA, Sagl) - Address of the company's operational headquarters in the Canton of Grisons - For a sole proprietorship: declaration of business start and identity document
### Contacts and Resources for Grisons
The competent office for registration with the commercial register in the Canton of Grisons is the Commercial Register of the Canton of Grisons at the Cantonal Administration. The canton provides updated forms, detailed instructions, and specific cost tables on its official website, which vary annually.
For federal tax issues (IFD, VAT), the Federal Customs Administration (AFC) is responsible. The first contact is usually the cantonal office of Grisons, which provides information on VAT registration and IFD number assignment.
### Next Steps and Practical Tools
Before proceeding with the registration, it is useful to calculate the tax and social security implications of the legal form choice. You can make a preliminary estimate of federal, cantonal, and municipal costs using the [tax and salary calculator](nav:calculator), which takes into account the legal form and assumed income. Additionally, many cantons, including Grisons, provide free checklists and guides on their official pages dedicated to entrepreneurs who wish to start a business in the territory.

## In a nutshell - Choose the legal form (sole proprietorship, company, Sàrl, SA) - Registration in the federal trade register via the cantonal office of Graubünden - Taxation at 3 levels: federal, cantonal, municipal - AVS/LPP obligations, LAMal and employee contributions
## Key facts - **What**: Procedure for opening a business in the Canton of Graubünden - Where: Canton of Graubünden, north-eastern Switzerland - Who: Founders, cantonal offices, tax authorities - System: Three levels of taxation (federal, cantonal, municipal) - Obligations: Health insurance (LAMal) and occupational pension (LPP)
Starting a business in the Canton of Graubünden requires a multi-level administrative process. The choice of legal form — from sole proprietorship to limited liability companies — is the first decisive step, followed by registration in the Federal Trade Register and registration with the Grison cantonal authorities. Each step has direct implications for taxation, pension and insurance obligations.
### Legal forms and their requirements
Switzerland recognises different legal forms for companies. The sole proprietorship is the simplest: it does not require minimum capital, but the owner is personally responsible for corporate debts. General partnerships and partnerships follow similar unlimited liability regimes, but involve multiple partners.
Capital companies — limited liability companies (Sàrl) and ## Taxation and social contributions: three levels, three obligations
Opening a business in the Canton of Graubünden means dealing with a three-level tax system: federal, cantonal, and municipal. This model, standard throughout Switzerland, creates a complex but transparent structure of levies and obligations.
### The three-level tax system
The Confederation collects the federal direct tax (IFD) on income and capital. Each canton — including Graubünden — applies its own cantonal taxes, and then the municipalities apply a multiplier to the cantonal income. This layering means that a company registered in the Canton of Graubünden will pay federal direct tax according to the federal progressive rate, cantonal tax of Graubünden according to the rates of cantonal legislation, and municipal tax with the multiplier set by the municipality where the company is located.
Each Swiss canton has full autonomy in setting its own rates. The Canton of Graubünden, like the other 25 cantons, independently defines its tax burdens. For this reason, companies with the same asset structure can pay very different taxes depending on the canton in which they are located.
### Insurance obligations and social contributions for employees
A company that employs staff (even just one) must register for unemployment insurance (AD) and acquire health insurance coverage (LAMal). For each employee, membership in a supplementary pension scheme (LPP) is mandatory, separate from the AVS (the first pillar of old-age, disability, and survivors' insurance).
Contributions per employee include: AVS/AI at 5.3% for the employee and 5.3% for the employer (total 10.6%), unemployment insurance at 1.1% up to an annual maximum, professional pension (LPP) according to age brackets (for example, 7% for the 25-34 age group) mainly at the employer's expense, and health insurance according to a private policy with monthly per capita premiums varying by canton and region. In the Canton of Graubünden, as throughout Switzerland, health insurance is not deducted from the salary as a percentage contribution but falls within the scope of mandatory private social protection. The LAMal remains binding for every resident regardless of income.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Practical checklist: the concrete steps to take
To turn an idea into an operational business in the Canton of Grisons, follow these concrete steps.
### 1. Choose your legal structure
Before any registration, decide whether to operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, or corporation. Each choice has legal, tax, and pension implications. A sole proprietorship is easy to start but exposes the owner to unlimited liability. An LLC requires more bureaucracy but offers asset protection.
### 2. Register the company in the commercial register
Contact the responsible office in the Canton of Grisons to submit the registration application. You will need a copy of the articles of association (for companies), identifying data of partners/managers, the legal address, and a brief description of the activity.
### 3. Register with the tax authorities
Once registered in the commercial register, the company is automatically reported to the federal and cantonal tax authorities. You will receive communications to obtain the taxpayer number. Also register with the cantonal tax office of Grisons for annual declarations.
### 4. Take out health insurance and join the pension scheme
If you hire employees, register with a health insurance provider for mandatory health coverage. Affiliate with a recognized professional pension institution for the LPP — this is mandatory for all companies with employees. Contributions start from the first day of employment and are based on the coordinated salary after federal deductions.
### 5. Register with the statistics office
In Switzerland, every company must register with the cantonal and federal statistics office for economic data collection purposes, according to the competencies of the FSO (Federal Statistical Office). This is an administrative obligation sometimes underestimated by new entrepreneurs.
It is not mandatory to rely on consultants, but it is recommended: an accountant experienced in Grisons cantonal tax law can correctly navigate tax, pension, and administrative obligations. The initial costs of consulting are offset by avoiding costly mistakes in the declaration phase. To calculate the overall costs and simulate the gross-net salary of the first employee, use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator). Subsequently, contact a tax office in the Canton of Grisons or an accounting firm directly to confirm the exact rates of your location and receive advice on any regional incentives for new businesses.

item.title: Opening businesses in the Canton of Graubünden: a complete guide
item.description: From the choice of legal form to the trade register: everything you need to know to start a business in the Canton of Graubünden.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Choice of legal form: sole proprietorship, company, cooperative - Mandatory registration in the cantonal commercial register - Insurance obligations: LAMal, AVS/AI, professional pension - Registration fees vary by form and canton
## Key facts - **What**: Starting a business in the Canton of Graubünden - Where: Canton of Graubünden, Switzerland - Who: Entrepreneurs, sole proprietorships, companies - When: Before starting the activity (within legal deadlines) - Capital: Varies by legal form (from zero for sole proprietorship) - Taxes: Vary by canton and legal form
### Starting a business in the Canton of Graubünden: the first steps
Opening a business in the Canton of Graubünden requires following a precise procedure set by Swiss law. The first step is choosing the legal form, a decision that conditions the legal structure, tax obligations, and personal risks of the entrepreneur.
In Switzerland, various legal forms are available: the sole proprietorship (the simplest and most common form), the general partnership (SNC), the limited partnership (SA), the joint-stock company (SA), the limited liability company (Sàrl), and the cooperative. Each form has different characteristics in terms of required minimum capital, personal liability, management structure, and administrative obligations.
Once the legal form is chosen, the entrepreneur must register their business in the commercial register of the Canton of Graubünden. The commercial register is a cantonal (not federal) register containing information about businesses registered in the territory. Registration is mandatory by law and must occur before starting commercial activity.
Registration in the register involves paying registration fees, the amount of which varies depending on the chosen legal form and the rates set by the Graubünden cantonal administration. There is no uniform national amount: each canton sets its own rates.
In addition to registration, those opening a business in the Canton of Graubünden must comply with insurance and pension obligations. First, as a resident in Switzerland (or employee), they must take out mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) within three months of arriving in Switzerland or starting the activity. Additionally, as a self-employed worker, they are subject to AVS/AI contributions for basic pension and must consider joining a professional pension fund (LPP/BVG) if not mandatory. It is also necessary to take out accident insurance (LAA/UVG) if the activity falls within sectors subject to this obligation. ### Legal forms and minimum capital
The choice of legal form is crucial for the structure of the business. A sole proprietorship does not require minimum capital and allows the entrepreneur to start with minimal personal funds, but it exposes them to unlimited liability towards creditors. On the other hand, corporations (SA, Sàrl) have minimum capital requirements and separate business assets from personal assets.
The public limited company (SA) and the limited liability company (Sàrl) are the most common for medium to large-sized activities. Both require a minimum capital stipulated by the Swiss Code of Obligations and vary depending on the chosen form. Cooperatives, on the other hand, are suitable for collective enterprises and have specific capital and governance rules.
Anyone starting a business must choose wisely: a sole proprietorship offers speed but exposes to personal risks. A corporation offers protection but requires more initial bureaucracy and tied-up capital. In the Canton of Grisons, as in every canton, the cantonal administration and local accountants can provide advice on the most suitable choice.
### Registration fees and administrative obligations
Registration in the commercial register involves registration fees, the amount of which is set by the Grisons cantonal authorities. In the Canton of Grisons, as in every canton, these amounts vary. There is no uniform national tariff: the Canton of Grisons has its own tariffs, which depend on the legal form and sometimes on the expected turnover. Consult the website of the cantonal commercial register office for updated figures.
In addition to the initial fees, anyone managing a business must comply with continuous administrative obligations: keeping accounts, submitting the annual tax return, paying taxes. Taxation in Switzerland is structured at three levels (federal, cantonal, municipal), and each level has its own rates and rules. In the Canton of Grisons, as in every canton, the municipalities apply multipliers to the cantonal rates, influencing the total tax burden. The federal administration (FTA) manages the federal direct tax and VAT at the national level, while the cantonal administrations manage cantonal and municipal taxes.
### Insurance and pension obligations
Anyone starting a business must be covered by compulsory health insurance (LAMal/KVG). Health insurance is private, and premiums vary based on age, gender, region of residence, and chosen deductible (CHF 300 to CHF 2.500 for adults). In the Canton of Grisons, as in every canton, the canton offers premium subsidies (premium reduction) for those with low income.
For pensions, the self-employed person must pay contributions to the AHV/AI at a fixed rate (about 5.3% for the worker, 10.6% total with the employer's part if they have a dual role) and, if subject, join a professional pension fund (LPP/BVG). Accident insurance (LAA/UVG) is mandatory for certain sectors with varying percentages (0.7–1.5% depending on the sector). These insurance obligations ensure personal protection and contribute to the Swiss social protection system (UFAS/BSV oversees pensions).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure: how to register with the commercial register
The procedure to start a business in the Canton of Graubünden is divided into well-defined phases that require attention to detail.
**Phase 1: Preliminary preparation.** Define the legal form (sole proprietorship, company, cooperative) based on the size and expected risks. Gather the necessary documents: for companies, draft the articles of association; for sole proprietorships, personal data and a dedicated bank account are sufficient. If you have employees, you must also comply with labor regulations (maximum 45 hours/week in industry/offices/sales, minimum 4 weeks of vacation, contributions for employees).
Phase 2: Registration with the commercial register. Contact the commercial register office of the Canton of Graubünden. Complete the provided registration forms and attach the required documents (copy of ID, constitutive documentation, etc.). Pay the registration fees according to the Graubünden cantonal tariff.
Phase 3: Tax registration. Once registered with the commercial register, the canton will communicate the data to the federal tax administration (FTA) and the cantonal administration. You will receive a federal identification number (UID) and must register as a taxpayer with the Canton of Graubünden. This number is essential for invoicing and declaring taxes.
Phase 4: Mandatory insurances. Immediately take out mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) within three months of starting the activity. Register with the cantonal AVS office for basic pension contributions. If necessary, join a professional pension fund (LPP/BVG) and, if applicable, insure against accidents (LAA/UVG) with SUVA or authorized insurers.
Phase 5: Accounting and taxation. Open a bank account dedicated to the activity. Implement an accounting system suitable for the legal form (simplified accounting for sole proprietorships, double-entry accounting for companies). Prepare the first balance sheet and the first tax return for the Canton of Graubünden and the federal administration, usually by March 31 of the following year.
### Critical deadlines
Registration with the commercial register must occur before starting the activity. Health insurance must be taken out within three months. The annual tax return must be submitted within the established deadlines (which vary slightly between cantons, but usually by March). Failure to comply with these obligations results in tax and administrative penalties.
### Practical tools for your business
Calculate the estimated annual taxes on your business income using [our federal and cantonal tax calculator](nav:calculator). If you compare the Canton of Graubünden with other cantons for the domicile of your company, you will notice significant differences in cantonal rates and municipal multipliers. Use [the AVS/LPP pension calculator](nav:pension) to estimate contributions based on expected income. For specific questions about the Graubünden commercial register and local procedures, contact the cantonal administration directly: each canton has slightly different procedures and requires periodic updates.

item.description: Complete guide to opening a business in the canton of Basel-City: legal forms, minimum capital, registration in the trade register, taxes and insurance.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Registration in the cantonal commercial register is mandatory before starting the activity - Choose the legal form: sole proprietorship, Ltd. (CHF 20'000), Corp. (CHF 100'000) - LAMal within 3 months; SUVA/LAA if you hire employees - Taxation on three levels: federal, cantonal, municipal
## Key facts - **What**: Registration in the commercial register (public archive managed by the canton) - Where: Canton of Basel-Stadt (cantonal administration) - Who: Founders of sole proprietorships, Ltd., Corp., cooperatives - Minimum capital: Corp. CHF 100'000; Ltd. CHF 20'000; sole proprietorship no limit - Obligations: LAMal (3 months), SUVA/LAA (employees), federal-cantonal-municipal taxation - Employee contributions: AHV/IV 5.3% (plus 5.3% employer), ALV 1.1% up to the maximum, LA 0.7–1.5% per sector
Anyone wishing to start a business in Switzerland — including in the canton of Basel-Stadt — must first register in the commercial register. It is not optional: registration is a federal legal obligation. Without it, the activity does not legally exist and cannot operate regularly. The commercial register is the fundamental public archive where all essential data of the company is documented: ownership, legal form, partners, capital, legal seats.
### What is the commercial register and why register The Swiss commercial register is a public database managed at the cantonal level. It contains information on sole proprietorships, Ltd. (Limited Liability Company), Corp. (Corporation), cooperatives, and other forms of organization. In Basel-Stadt, registration is the responsibility of the dedicated cantonal administration.
Registration allows the public administration to verify the existence and legitimacy of the company, trace ownership and responsibilities, and is essential for accessing bank credit, entering into commercial contracts, and operating regularly within the cantonal territory.
### The main legal forms The choice of legal form is critical as it determines the minimum capital, personal liability, and tax structure. In Switzerland, the three most common forms are:
- Sole proprietorship: A single natural person manages the activity in their own name. There is no minimum capital required. Liability is unlimited (personal assets are at risk in case of business debts). It is the simplest form bureaucratically.
- Limited Liability Company (Ltd.): One or more partners. Minimum capital: CHF 20'000. Liability is limited to the capital contributed. More formal and protective than the sole proprietorship. Requires a constitutive act drafted by a notary.
- Corporation (Corp.): One or more shareholders. Minimum capital: CHF 100'000. Maximum protection of personal liability (private assets remain separate). More complex, expensive, and bureaucratic form, suitable for larger companies or investment structures.
In Basel-Stadt, as in the rest of the canton, registration in the commercial register takes place at the competent cantonal office (Handelsregister Basel-Stadt). The exact procedures and deadlines vary by canton: ask for specific information directly from the Basel-Stadt administration for rates, registration fees, and precise times. ### Insurance and Contribution Obligations
Opening a business in Switzerland means subjecting yourself to federal and cantonal social security and insurance obligations that cannot be omitted.
**LAMal (Mandatory Health Insurance)**
All Swiss residents must take out health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of arrival or the start of the activity. For founders and employees of a new company, this means contracting with a private authorized health insurance fund. Premiums are individual (per capita), not taxes or salary contributions deducted from the salary. Each fund offers different deductibles (CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500) and premiums that vary by canton and risk region. Cantons provide subsidies to reduce premiums for low-income brackets: ask the Basel-Stadt administration for specific amounts.
SUVA and Accident Insurance (LAA)
If you hire employees, you are required to take out professional accident insurance. SUVA (Swiss National Accident Insurance Institute) or other authorized companies (LAA) offer policies. The contribution is exclusively the employer's responsibility and ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% of the employee's salary, depending on the activity sector. No contribution is deducted from the employee.
Mandatory Pension Contributions for Employees
For each employee, you must pay contributions to the Swiss pension system, divided between the employer and the worker: - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% at the employee's expense, 5.3% at the employer's expense (total 10.6%). These fund old-age pensions (AVS), disability insurance (AI), and maternity/paternity allowances (IPG). - Unemployment Insurance (AD): Approximately 1.1% up to an annual maximum, divided between the employee and the employer. - LPP (Pension Fund, second pillar): Mandatory for coordinated salaries. The employer contributes a percentage that varies by age group: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ until the reference age).
These contributions are deducted from salaries and paid to the funds by you as the employer. They are mandatory for any employed worker.
### Taxation: Three Independent Levels
Taxation in Switzerland operates on three independent and simultaneous levels:
1. Federal Direct Tax (IFD): Managed by ESTV (Federal Customs Administration). National progressive rate applied at the federal level. 2. Cantonal Taxes: Each canton has its own rates and tax laws according to its fiscal priorities. Basel-Stadt has its specific rates. 3. Municipal Taxes: Municipalities multiply the cantonal rate according to local rules (municipal multiplier coefficient).
For a new activity, taxation depends on the legal form: - Sole Proprietorship: The income is taxed as the founder's personal income on all three rates (federal + cantonal + municipal). - LLC and Corporation: The legal entity is fiscally separate and taxed as an autonomous entity at the federal, cantonal, and municipal levels based on income and profits.
The specific rates for Basel-Stadt canton vary according to cantonal fiscal policy: ask the Basel-Stadt cantonal tax administration (Finanzbehörde Basel-Stadt) or a tax consultant for updated percentages. Once the activity is registered, you will have to file annual tax returns both at the federal level (ESTV) and cantonal level.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Practical procedure: 7 steps to start your business
Step 1: Choose the legal form Decide whether to operate as a sole proprietorship (simpler, unlimited liability), SARL (minimum capital CHF 20,000, limited liability) or SA (minimum capital CHF 100,000, maximum protection). Consult a notary or legal advisor to align the choice with your situation, expected turnover, and risk tolerance.
Step 2: Acquire the minimum capital (if SARL or SA) For SARL, CHF 20,000 must be paid in; for SA, CHF 100,000. The capital must be deposited with a Swiss bank, certified, and documented. For a sole proprietorship, there is no legal minimum capital, but sufficient means are still required to start the business.
**Step 3: Prepare founding documents** For a sole proprietorship: few documents (identity, address, activity description). For SARL: articles of association, internal regulations, list of shareholders. For SA: statutes, list of shareholders, bank deposit certificate. A notary can assist in drafting and certifying.
Step 4: Register with the Basel-Stadt commercial register Contact the Basel-Stadt commercial register office with the founding documents, founders' identities, legal address, and bank deposit certificate of the capital (for SARL and SA). Deadlines and the exact process vary: contact the cantonal office directly for exact times and specific registration fees in Basel-Stadt.
Step 5: Register with LAMal within 3 months You and each employee must take out LAMal health insurance within 3 months of registration. Choose a health insurance company, communicate the start of the activity and personal data. Premiums are individual and depend on the canton, age, and income bracket. Request information on possible cantonal subsidies for your income.
Step 6: Take out SUVA or LAA (if you hire employees) If you will have employees, register with SUVA or an authorized private accident insurance within specific times. Communicate the employees' data, their salaries, and the sector of activity for the calculation of the contribution (0.7–1.5% of the salary).
Step 7: Federal and cantonal tax registration Once registered with the commercial register, ESTV and the Basel-Stadt tax administration will contact you for VAT registration (if annual turnover > CHF 100,000) and for cantonal direct federal tax. Complete the provided forms and meet the deadlines for the annual declaration of your activity.
### Final checklist before starting
- ✓ Legal form chosen and documented - ✓ Minimum capital deposited and certified (if SARL/SA) - ✓ Founding documents prepared - ✓ Registration with the Basel-Stadt commercial register completed - ✓ LAMal taken out for all (founders and employees) - ✓ SUVA/LAA activated (if employees present) - ✓ ESTV and cantonal tax administration registration completed - ✓ First fiscal year planned and deadlines noted
For exact figures, specific cantonal deadlines, registration fees, and concrete administrative details related to Basel-Stadt, contact the commercial register office (Handelsregister Basel-Stadt) and the cantonal tax administration (Finanzbehörde) directly. Consider having a notary or legal advisor assist you during the first process: the initial cost pays off in clarity and regulatory compliance.
Use our [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation based on expected income and chosen legal form. You will better understand the tax impact of your activity and plan the operating budget.

item.title: Naturalization Basel City: requirements and procedure
item.description: Complete guide to the federal and cantonal requirements for ordinary naturalization in the Canton of Basel-City, from documents to language tests.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Ordinary naturalization: permit C + 10 years federal residence - Basel City applies specific cantonal and municipal requirements - German language test (Swiss standard) usually required - Taxes and procedures vary between municipalities
## Key facts - **What**: Ordinary naturalization with C permit for at least 10 years - Where: Canton Basel City (municipalities: Basel, Riehen, Bettingen, others) - Who: Foreigners with a C permit established for at least 10 years - Requirements: Socio-cultural integration, knowledge of German language - Procedure: Question to the municipality, cantonal assessment - Taxes: Amounts defined by each municipality
### The federal framework of ordinary naturalization
Ordinary naturalization in Switzerland is based on stable federal criteria: those who wish to acquire Swiss citizenship must have had a C (domicile) permit for at least ten years. In the Canton of Basel-City, the competent municipalities (Basel, Riehen, Bettingen and others) add their own requirements in addition to federal legislation.
The procedure begins with an application submitted to the municipality of residence, which then forwards the application to the cantonal authorities for final assessment. Integration and German language tests constitute ordinary components in the assessment, although the details and modalities vary according to the municipality concerned.
### Who can access ordinary naturalization
Swiss federal law states that a foreign person may access ## Cantonal and Municipal Procedures in Basel-Stadt In the Canton of Basel-Stadt, the naturalization procedure is not uniform for all municipalities. Each municipality (Basel, Riehen, Bettingen, Birsfelden, and others) defines specific modalities and timelines, although the reference framework remains federal. The application must be submitted with a series of standard documents: extract from the residents' register, certificate of good conduct, evidence of integration (work, volunteering, civic participation), proof of language knowledge. Some municipalities may require additional certificates related to economic, family, or housing situations. Once the application is submitted to the municipality, it undergoes a publication phase (opposition period) during which citizens and authorities can raise objections. If there are no significant objections, the file is passed to the cantonal authorities for final approval. ### Naturalization Fees and Amounts The fees for naturalization vary significantly between Swiss municipalities and even within the same canton. In the Canton of Basel-Stadt, each municipality applies its own amounts, which generally range from a few hundred to a few thousand Swiss francs. It is essential to verify the current amounts directly with the municipality of residence, as these can change annually. Some municipalities offer the possibility to pay the fees in installments, but this option varies from municipality to municipality. Contact your municipal office to learn about the available payment methods. ### Procedure Timeline The overall timeline from the submission of the application to the final approval depends on multiple factors: completeness of the documentation, results of language and integration tests, number of files being processed by the municipality and the canton, any objections during the publication phase. On average, the process takes months (not days), but the Canton of Basel-Stadt has not publicly communicated standardized fixed deadlines. It is prudent to expect variable times depending on the municipality and the season (some periods present higher workloads). ### Fiscal Implications and Post-Naturalization Benefits Once naturalized, you will have access to the same fiscal benefits and duties as Swiss citizens. This includes the annual obligation to submit the federal and cantonal direct tax return through the [tax return procedure](nav:tax-return), the right to participate in federal, cantonal, and municipal votes, and full social and pension rights (including AHV and LPP). ### Appeals and Recourses in Case of Denial If a naturalization application is rejected, it is possible to appeal to the competent cantonal authorities within specific deadlines (usually 30 days from the denial). The appeal must detail the reasons why you believe the decision is incorrect or unfair. The cantonal authorities will review your file according to the formal procedure provided.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Step-by-step operational procedure
Step 1: Verify federal prerequisites. Ensure you have held a C permit (residence) for at least ten years. If your residence in Switzerland is less than this limit, you will have to wait. Certain periods (e.g., 8-18 years) count double according to federal regulations, thus reducing the overall time.
Step 2: Contact your municipality. Identify the competent office in the municipality where you reside (civil registry office, naturalization administrative office, or similar). Basel-Stadt includes Basel, Riehen, Bettingen, Birsfelden, Bottmingen, Münchenstein, and other municipalities: each has a specific point of contact. Request the required documentation and submission methods.
Step 3: Gather the necessary documents. Prepare a recent extract from the residents' register (generally not older than 3 months), a certificate of good conduct, proof of work and civic integration, and certificates of knowledge of Swiss German. The municipality may request additional documents based on your situation.
**Step 4: Submit the application.** Submit the complete application to the municipality, preferably in person or according to the communicated methods. Ensure you include all required documentation and receive a submission receipt.
Step 5: Wait for the publication phase. The municipality will publish your application for a set period (generally 30-60 days). During this period, anyone can raise justified objections regarding your eligibility or integration issues.
Step 6: Pass the tests (if required). If the municipality requires it, you must take the Swiss German language test and the integration test according to the methods and dates communicated by the office.
Step 7: Cantonal approval and issuance of the certificate. If everything proceeds positively and there are no objections, the file is forwarded to the cantonal authorities for final approval. Once approved, you will receive the Swiss citizenship certificate.
## Practical tools and resources
For detailed information specific to your municipality in Basel-Stadt, contact the competent municipal offices directly. The canton and municipalities provide online guides and telephone support. Federal resources (SEM - State Secretariat for Migration) offer overviews of the standard federal procedure.
[Use our tax calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the tax impact of naturalization on your income situation in Switzerland and understand how your contribution obligations will change.
If you currently work as a cross-border commuter and reside in another country, consult our in-depth analysis on [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to evaluate your post-naturalization economic budget.
If you are looking for [new job opportunities](nav:jobs) after naturalization, you will be able to access the Swiss job market without restrictions due to residence permits.
## Practical checklist for naturalization
- ☐ Verify your status: C permit for 10 years? (Periods 8-18 years count double) - ☐ Contact your municipality of residence - ☐ Request the official list of required documents - ☐ Prepare extract from the register and certificates of good conduct - ☐ Gather proof of socio-cultural and work integration - ☐ Schedule the language test if required by the municipality - ☐ Submit the complete application and keep the receipt
