item.title: Soletta rental market: fees and rental rights
item.description: Complete Guide to the Right of Tenancy in the Canton of Solothurn: Federal Rules on Security Deposit, Cancellation, Rent Dispute and Conciliation Authority.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Maximum 3 months' rent deposit, blocked account in the tenant's name - Landlord's notice only on official cantonal form - Challenge the rent within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Federal law identical throughout Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Federal tenancy law (Code of Obligations, art. 253 et seq.) - Where: Canton of Solothurn and all of Switzerland - Security deposit: Maximum 3 months' rent - Challenge deadline: 30 days from receipt of the proposal - Notice procedure: Mandatory official cantonal form
The rental market in the Canton of Solothurn, like the rest of Switzerland, is governed by a uniform federal legal framework. Regardless of the geographical area or region, anyone renting or occupying a property enjoys the same rights and obligations established by the Code of Obligations (CO) from article 253 onwards. This means that tenants and landlords do not find regulatory differences between the Canton of Solothurn and other Swiss cantons: the rental rules remain the same from Basel to Lugano, from Zurich to Geneva.
Swiss tenancy law is based on three fundamental pillars: the protection of the security deposit, the correct procedures for terminating the contract, and the possibility of challenging a rent deemed unfair through a local conciliation authority. Knowing these rights is essential to protect yourself and your family from unfair commercial practices.
### The security deposit: guaranteed protection
When a tenant rents a property, the landlord or their real estate agency may require a security deposit. Federal law sets a clear and non-negotiable limit: the deposit may not exceed three months' rent. This limit applies in all cantons, without exception.
The deposit must be paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name and managed so that the amount is always accessible and protected from risks. The landlord cannot use the deposit to cover overdue rent, condominium expenses, or damages during the tenancy: it serves only as a guarantee for any damages to the property found at the end of the contract. Monthly rents are two completely separate costs. To correctly assess whether the proposed rent is sustainable within your budget, [consult our cost of living analysis tool in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living).
### Notice: strict and mandatory form
When the landlord decides to terminate the contract, the notice must be given on an official form provided by the Canton of Solothurn. An informal letter, an email communication, or a telephone conversation is not sufficient: the form is strict. Failure to comply with the official form renders the notice null and void, as if it had never occurred. This is one of the most important points to remember, as many landlords still believe that a generic written communication is sufficient for termination.
The notice periods vary according to the year of tenancy — according to federal law — but the procedure remains the same: official form, respect of the deadlines, certified communication to the tenant. Challenging the rent and appealing to the conciliation authority are the most important tools for tenants to protect themselves in cases of excessive rents or unjustified increases. This right is explicitly stated in the Federal Code of Obligations and applies to everyone, from the first tenant to the elderly person moving house. It is not a privilege but a concrete right protected by law.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How to proceed step by step
Phase 1: Receiving the rent proposal When the owner or agency proposes an initial rent, the tenant receives a written communication with the requested amount. At this point, they have 30 days to decide whether to accept or contest it. It is advisable to keep all documentation, including the date of receipt of the proposal, as this date starts the countdown of the terms.
**Phase 2: Evaluating the proposal** Before deciding, the tenant must evaluate whether the rent is reasonable compared to rents in their neighborhood for apartments of similar size, amenities (heating, hot water, elevator, garden), and location. For this evaluation, it is useful to consult local real estate listings, contact owners of similar properties, or seek advice from a tenants' association in the canton.
Phase 3: Preparing the contestation If the tenant finds the rent unfair, they must file a formal appeal with the conciliation authority of the Canton of Solothurn. The appeal must include: the complete address and square footage of the property, a description of the amenities, the requested rent, comparable reference rents with justification, a written explanation of the contestation, and the tenant's contact information (name, address, phone, email).
Phase 4: Filing within the deadline The tenant submits the appeal to the conciliation authority within 30 days of receiving the rent proposal. Attached documents: a copy of the owner's rent proposal, comparative documentation (printed market listings or certificates), copies of any previous communications between the parties, and supporting attachments (property valuations, reports from tenants' associations). The appeal must be sent in writing, according to the canton's authority's methods (paper, email, or online portal if available).
Phase 5: Conciliation procedure The authority summons the parties (owner and tenant) for a joint hearing on an agreed date, usually within 2-4 weeks of the appeal's filing. Both parties present their reasons orally and in writing. The authority asks clarifying questions, reviews the submitted documentation, and evaluates the reasonableness of both parties' positions. At the end, the authority proposes a compromise amount and attempts to mediate to reach an agreement.
Phase 6: Outcome and further actions If the parties reach an agreement during the conciliation, a conciliation record is drawn up, which is binding on both. If there is no agreement, the authority issues a conciliation report with a proposed solution. The parties then have the right to appeal to the civil court if they are not satisfied with the authority's report.
### Where to go in the Canton of Solothurn The Canton of Solothurn has an office or commission for conciliation in rental matters. The address, opening hours, and contact methods are available from the Department of Justice and Security of the canton or from the tenant's municipality of residence. Many municipalities in Solothurn also have local offices dedicated to these procedures.
### Costs and times of the procedure The conciliation procedure is generally low-cost for the tenant, sometimes free or with symbolic fees for both parties. The times vary from two to six months, depending on the complexity of the dispute, the availability of the parties, and the workload of the conciliation authority. In case of appeal to the judge after failed conciliation, the times extend by additional months or years.
To better understand how rents fit into your overall budget in Switzerland and to evaluate the sustainability of a rent in your personal and family context, [consult our cost of living analysis tool in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living). This will allow you to contextualize the rent compared to your income and other monthly expenses.

item.title: Buying a house in the canton of Graubünden: mortgage, costs and procedures
item.description: Practical guide to buying real estate in Graubünden: purchase and sale procedures, own funds required, mortgage loan sustainability, transfer taxes and notary fees.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Buying a house in Switzerland requires own funds (20-30% of the price) - Transfer taxes and notary fees vary by canton - Mortgage loan subject to bank sustainability check
## Key facts - **What**: Acquisition of a residential property - When: Process usually takes 2-4 months (from preliminary agreement to notarial signing) - Where: Canton of Graubünden, Switzerland - Who: Buyer, seller, notary, and bank - Amount: Own funds minimum 20-30% of the price (Swiss market standard)
Buying a house in the canton of Graubünden follows the national Swiss legal procedure, marked by precise phases: preliminary agreement, property inspection, title verification, final contract, property transfer. The system is regulated at the federal level for contractual aspects (Code of Obligations), but taxes and costs vary significantly between cantons.
The canton of Graubünden, like every Swiss canton, has its own tax levels: federal direct tax (FDT), cantonal tax, and municipal taxes constitute the three tax levels in the Swiss system. In the real estate purchase process, the relevant taxes are mainly the transfer tax at the time of notarial signing and the notary fees, which vary depending on the transaction amount. Municipal taxation adds a multiplier to the cantonal rates.
### Financing structure
A property is purchased by combining own funds and mortgage credit. Own funds are the amount the buyer must pay out of pocket, usually not less than 20% of the purchase price in the Swiss market. This amount is not subject to strict federal law but represents the standard required by banks to approve a mortgage. Exceeding 20-30% of own funds reduces the debt ratio and improves financing conditions.
The remaining amount (70-80% of the price) is financed through a mortgage loan secured by the property itself. The mortgage is provided by banks and specialized credit institutions. In the Swiss system, the mortgage is subject to a sustainability check: the bank simulates the cost of the monthly installment as if the interest rate were higher, to ensure that the borrower can meet the payment even in case of interest rate hikes. [Check the amount of your gross income on your payslip](nav:payslip) before contacting a bank for pre-financing. ### Sustainability Assessment
The sustainability of the mortgage is calculated by the bank based on the gross income of the buyer. In Switzerland, banks use an empirical rule: the monthly mortgage installment, added to other housing expenses (heating, maintenance, homeowner's insurance), should not exceed 33% of the gross monthly income. This is a market standard, not a federal law, but it is uniformly applied by all credit institutions.
In the calculation, net and gross salary (from pay slips and income certificates), any additional income (rent, pensions), federal, cantonal, and municipal income taxes are considered. The canton of Graubünden, like every Swiss canton, has its own cantonal tax rates. The bank also evaluates the requested mortgage amount, the reference interest rate, and the duration of the financing (usually 15-25 years).
The bank also conducts a credit check through the central debt data used by Swiss institutions and requires complete documentation: last 2 years of tax returns, income certificates from the employer, updated personal balance sheet.
### Taxes and Direct Costs
At the time of the notarial signing, the buyer is required to pay the transfer tax, calculated on the purchase price. There is no federal transfer tax, but it is the responsibility of the canton (and partly the municipality) to collect this tax based on their own rates. The canton of Graubünden, as an autonomous territorial entity with tax competence, sets the rates for its own transfer tax.
Notary fees vary by canton and by the amount of the sale, generally from 0.5% to 1% of the purchase price. The drafting of the authentic deed (mandatory in Switzerland for real estate) is carried out by the notary. Some cantons add a land tax to the transfer of ownership.
In addition to these direct costs, the real estate appraisal (required by the bank, about 0.5%-1% of the property value), homeowner's insurance (mandatory for every real estate), and registration in the land register (notary fee included) must be considered. [Calculate the sustainability of your mortgage](nav:calculator) using our estimation tool.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### The step-by-step procedure
Phase 1: Search and preliminary promise. Identify the property through a real estate agent or directly from the owner. Once the property is found, a preliminary promise is signed (not mandatory, but common in Switzerland): it is a non-binding document that blocks the property for a few weeks while the buyer verifies the financing with the bank.
**Phase 2: Financing verification.** Contact the bank for a pre-approval of the mortgage. The bank requires income documentation (last 2 years of tax returns), imposes a real estate appraisal, verifies the sustainability of the mortgage in relation to your income. This step takes 3-4 weeks. Only then do you receive a pre-approval letter from the bank.
Phase 3: Definitive contract. Once pre-approval is obtained, the buyer and seller sign the purchase contract before a notary. The notary drafts the document in authentic form (mandatory for real estate in Switzerland) and registers the transfer in the Cantonal Land Register of Graubünden.
Phase 4: Mortgage disbursement and payment. The bank disburses the mortgage to the notary (who holds it in deposit). The buyer pays the own funds. The notary pays the seller and the transfer of ownership is completed. The buyer receives the registration notice in the Register and becomes the formal owner.
### Essential documents to prepare
Before contacting a bank, prepare the last 2-3 years of tax returns (federal and cantonal), income certificates from the employer (last 12 months), bank statement (last 3-6 months), latest pay slip (last 3 months), valid identity document, marriage certificate if applicable, extract from the Central Debt Register. These documents are mandatory for the bank's creditworthiness assessment.
### When to consult a specialist
It is advisable to be accompanied by a real estate agent during the search (not mandatory but useful to know the local market of the canton of Graubünden) and by a notary (mandatory for the signing of the authentic contract). Some buyers also use a tax consultant to understand the cantonal and municipal tax implications of the purchase in the canton of Graubünden, especially if the income is complex.
To get started, [consult the tax and purchase cost calculator](nav:calculator) for a preliminary estimate or contact a bank for mortgage pre-approval.

item.title: Nursery and childcare in the Canton of Graubünden
item.description: Custody options, income-based fees and cantonal subsidies: a practical guide for families in Graubünden.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Three main options: daycare, family daycare, after-school care - Fees calculated based on the family's gross income according to cantonal scales - Cantonal subsidies available for families below defined income limits - Access through the cantonal family office and direct registration with the facilities
## Key facts - **What**: Childcare services for preschool and school-age children (daycare, family daycare, after-school care) - Where: Canton of Grisons and other Swiss cantons - Who: Authorized public/private facilities, specialized educators, cantonal welfare offices - Amount: Variable monthly fees per canton and facility (income-based fee scale) - Access: Contact cantonal office, submit income documentation, direct registration
Finding reliable childcare during working hours is a concrete priority for Swiss families. In the Canton of Grisons, as in other cantons, the available options are diverse: daycare for the youngest, family daycare with private educators, and after-school care for school-age children. A central element is that the fees do not follow a fixed rate but are calculated based on the family's gross income, with public subsidy systems designed to make access to services more equitable.
Understanding how these services work, identifying real costs, and accessing cantonal contributions can make a significant difference in the household budget. A family with two incomes does not bear the same economic burden as a single-income family, and in many cases, public subsidies cover a significant portion of the monthly fee.
### The three main childcare options
In the Canton of Grisons, three main categories of childcare services are distinguished.
Daycare: Authorized public or private facilities that welcome children from the end of parental leave (typically from three months) until they start kindergarten. Daycare centers provide a structured environment with specialized educators, dedicated spaces, play activities, and meals. Standard hours are from 7:00 AM to 6:00 PM, with variations depending on the facility and calendar.
Family daycare: Children are entrusted to the home of a registered and authorized educator (institutions known as dagheimerin or dagos in local dialect). This option offers greater flexibility in hours and generally accommodates fewer children than collective daycare centers. Family daycare providers must comply with cantonal standards for training and safety.
After-school care: Services for children attending primary school, operating from 11:30 AM/12:00 PM to approximately 6:00 PM on school days. They include lunch, supervised homework, recreational activities, and supervision.
### How fees are calculated
Fees are not uniform but vary directly with the family's gross income. This principle, common to almost all Swiss cantons, aims to ensure equity in access to public services. A family with an annual gross income of CHF 40,000 bears a much lower cost than a family with CHF 120,000.
The calculation is made using a cantonal fee scale that considers the declared gross income, the composition of the family unit (number of children in care, number of working parents), and sometimes the movable or immovable assets. The result is a percentage of the daily or monthly cost that the family must pay directly.
In the most transparent systems, the facility provides an online preliminary simulation: a family enters their income in a form and receives an indication of the net monthly fee (already net of subsidies, if eligible) before signing the contract. ### Cantonal subsidies and family support
In addition to income-based fees, the Canton of Graubünden, like most Swiss cantons, provides **direct subsidies** for families whose income falls below certain levels or who have documented special needs.
The subsidy covers a variable percentage at the cantonal level: in some cases from 30 to 50% of the fee, in others up to 100% for the most vulnerable families. Access requires the submission of the most recent tax return and any other documents attesting to income (pay slips, statements from pension funds, self-employed declarations). The canton evaluates the request and, if approved, communicates the monthly contribution to the parent, who applies it directly to the facility's invoice.
This system allows many families to access childcare services that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive. Where a couple of teachers might benefit from a modest subsidy, a single-income family with an average income receives a more substantial contribution.
### Practical scenarios: how real costs vary
The difference between a single-income family and a dual-income family is significant.
Case 1 — Single-income family: One working parent (gross income CHF 50,000/year) and a two-year-old child. The childcare facility offers a base fee of CHF 1,800 per month. According to the cantonal income scale, the family pays 35% of the fee (CHF 630), while the cantonal subsidy covers the remaining 65% (CHF 1,170). The net cost is CHF 630 per month, or one-third of the nominal fee.
Case 2 — Dual-income couple: Both parents work with combined incomes of CHF 140,000/year and a three-year-old child in daycare. The base fee remains CHF 1,800, but they do not qualify for public subsidies (income above eligibility limits). They pay the full fee: CHF 1,800 per month. In this context, the cost is almost three times higher than in Case 1.
Case 3 — Single-income family with two children: One parent (CHF 35,000/year) with two children, one in daycare and one in after-school care. The total fee for both facilities is CHF 2,500 per month. With cantonal subsidies and a favorable fee scale for low-income families, the family pays CHF 400 (16% of the expense), and the canton covers the remaining CHF 2,100.
These scenarios illustrate how the system is structured to not exclude lower-income families and to significantly reduce the burden on single-income families, while maintaining shared economic responsibility.
### Factors influencing the choice of facility
In addition to cost, families consider extended opening hours (some facilities remain open until 19:00 or 20:00 for parents with shifts), geographical location relative to the workplace, pedagogical orientation (Montessori method, Waldorf approach, traditional proposal), educator-child ratio, and availability of spots. Some facilities accept children with specific needs (documented allergies, inclusive support for disabilities); others do not. Finding the ideal facility requires time and the evaluation of multiple criteria simultaneously.
A practical tip: contact the cantonal office for a complete and up-to-date list of all authorized facilities in your district; many cantonal administrations also offer a brief description of their distinctive features.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to search for a custodial facility in the Canton of Graubün
The first recommended step is to contact the relevant cantonal office — usually the Social Service Office, the Family Office or the equivalent welfare office. This body keeps an up-to-date register of all public and private services authorised in the canton, with information on availability, timetables, teaching languages (Graubünden is characterised by mainly German-speaking areas, but also includes Romance and Italian areas), and available staff.
The cantonal office also provides detailed guidance on how to access benefits and what documentation to submit. Although it is not mandatory to contact this entity, it is highly recommended to do so before undertaking independent research, as it avoids unproductive research and clarifies your eligibility for public contributions immediately.

item.title: New car sales down in August, almost one in three is electric
item.description: Sales of new cars in Switzerland fell by 0.6% in August, with almost one in three cars sold electric.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - New car sales in Switzerland decreased by 0.6% in August. - Almost one in three cars sold is electric. - Hybrid cars account for 37% of sales.
## Key facts - **What**: Decline in new car sales - When: August 2026 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Auto-Switzerland - Amount: 16,000 vehicles
New car sales in Switzerland recorded a 0.6% decrease in August, with 16,000 vehicles registered, according to the importers' association Auto-Switzerland. This figure represents a decline compared to the same period last year, which was already weak. Alternative drives reached a market share of 79%, with a significant increase in electric cars, which account for 30% of sales, up from 20% the previous year. Conventional hybrid cars are at 37%, while gasoline cars have fallen to 16% and diesels to 5%.
### Sales Details
In detail, conventional hybrid cars maintained a 37% share, a slight increase from 36% the previous year. Electric cars saw a significant increase, rising from 20% to 30% of the market, with 4800 cars registered, a 49% increase. Plug-in hybrids remained stable at 12%. Gasoline cars fell from 24% to 16%, while diesels decreased from 7% to 5%.
Overall, in the first eight months of 2026, 151,600 vehicles were registered, an increase of 1.8% compared to the same period last year. Hybrid cars reached 55,600 units, an increase of 2%, while electric cars saw a 23% increase with 37,600 units. Gasoline cars decreased by 16% to 31,200 units, while plug-in hybrids increased by 17% to 18,800 units. Diesels decreased by 24% to 8400 units. The share of 4x4s increased from 50% to 53%.
### Industry Comments
"The August data confirms that the sector's situation remains very tense," commented Auto-Switzerland director Thomas Rücker. "The overall very weak market trend negatively impacts the prospects for new vehicle trade." Rücker emphasized the urgency of deregulation and greater flexibility in CO2 emission regulations, in line with the rest of Europe. He also warned that new taxes or regulatory burdens on electric vehicles would have a counterproductive effect, stating that "any additional tax is inappropriate."
### Brand Ranking
Volkswagen led with 17,000 vehicles sold between January and August, followed by Skoda with 14,200, BMW with 12,500, Mercedes with 12,100, Audi with 10,200, Toyota with 8800, Volvo with 5700, Seat/Cupra with 5700, Renault with 5400, Dacia with 4900, Hyundai with 4600, KIA with 4000, BYD with 3900, Tesla with 3400, Ford with 3200, and Peugeot with 3200. All other manufacturers did not reach 3000 units. ### Practical Implications

item.title: Driving license in Freiburg: conversion and exams
item.description: Procedure for converting a foreign driver's license in the Canton of Freiburg: compulsory courses, theoretical and practical exams, required documents and step-by-step roadmaps.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The foreign license is not automatically valid: it requires cantonal conversion - Mandatory procedure: courses, theoretical exam, practical exam - Competent authority: Office of the circulation of the Canton of Fribourg - Times and costs vary; consult the local office
## Key facts - **What**: Conversion of foreign license in the Canton of Fribourg - Who: Office of the circulation of the Canton of Fribourg - Where: Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland - When: From arrival and registration of residence - Legal level: Cantonal ordinances on road traffic - Mandatory components: Courses, theoretical exam, practical exam
The driving license is an essential document for those residing or working in Switzerland. If you arrive in the Canton of Fribourg with a driving license issued by a foreign country — whether it is a country of the European Union, a third country, or a different Swiss canton — you will quickly discover that it is not automatically recognized for driving in the Fribourg territory.
The reason is simple: in Switzerland, the competencies on road traffic, driving licenses, exams, and conversions of foreign licenses fall under cantonal jurisdiction. There is no "national" Swiss license; each canton manages its own license system according to specific cantonal ordinances. Fribourg is no exception. The Canton has developed its own process for the conversion of foreign licenses, which includes a series of preparatory courses, a theoretical exam on road signs and Swiss regulations, and a practical driving exam. These are not optional.
### Who is responsible and where to go
The Office of the circulation of the Canton of Fribourg is the competent institution for all matters related to driving licenses, conversions, renewals, and administrative sanctions. It is at this office that you must submit an application for conversion, provide the required documents, enroll in courses, and book exams. Contacting the circulation office directly is the first mandatory step: you can receive information on processing times, administrative fees, available courses, and exam dates.
Even if you come from a member country of the European Union, with which Switzerland has free movement agreements, your license is not automatically valid permanently in the canton of Fribourg. Technical standards, road signs, and traffic codes can differ significantly; the conversion ensures that you actually know the local rules and can drive safely on Swiss alpine and urban roads. ## The three pillars of conversion: courses, theoretical exam, practical exam
The procedure for converting a foreign licence in the Canton of Freiburg is divided into three distinct and mandatory phases, each with a specific purpose.
** Compulsory preparatory courses ** Before taking the exams, the applicant must attend preparation courses organised by bodies authorised by the canton. The courses address specific topics of the Swiss and Freiburg reality: Swiss road signs, speed limits, rules of conduct on mountain roads, vehicle equipment obligations (winter chains, danger triangles, high-visibility vests), and road safety regulations. These courses are not optional; their attendance is a necessary condition to access the official exams.
Theoretical examination The theoretical examination tests knowledge of Swiss and cantonal road traffic regulations. It is generally conducted in written or digital form, with multiple-choice questions. It covers the international signs adopted by Switzerland, the road code, correct behaviour in critical situations (fog, snowfall, aquaplaning), specific driving rules on alpine passes, and other aspects of Swiss roads. Passing this exam is a prerequisite to access the practical exam.
Practical exam After passing the theoretical examination, the applicant takes a practical driving test with an official examiner from the canton.

Step 1: Contact the traffic office The first step is to submit an official conversion request to the traffic office of the Canton of Fribourg. You can contact them in person at their headquarters, by letter, or through the canton's online portal (if available). The office will provide you with the complete list of required documents, the administrative fees to be paid, and an indicative calendar of available courses. Do not hesitate to ask specific questions about timing and costs.
Step 2: Gather documents and pay fees Prepare all required documents: foreign driver's license, identity document, proof of residence. Pay the administrative fees set by the canton to the traffic office (amount not yet specified; verify with the office). This step is a prerequisite for enrolling in courses. Keep payment receipts and document submission certifications for future reference.
Step 3: Enroll in preparation courses The traffic office provides a list of authorized entities offering preparation courses. Choose the provider and date that suits you best, and formally enroll. Courses may be offered in Italian, French, or German, depending on the provider. Confirm the start date, duration, and documentation required for attendance.
Step 4: Attend courses and obtain the certificate Participate in all mandatory courses and obtain the official attendance certificate. This certificate is required to book the theoretical exam. Do not miss classes; absence may require repeating the entire course.
Step 5: Book and take the theoretical exam Once you have received the attendance certificate, contact the traffic office to book the theoretical exam. The date will be assigned according to the office's availability. Study Swiss regulations well before the exam. If you pass the theoretical exam, you can proceed to the next step; if you fail, you can retake it within the allowed number of attempts.
Step 6: Book and take the practical exam After passing the theoretical exam, you can book the practical driving exam. Dates are subject to availability. The exam is conducted with a vehicle provided by the office or, in some cases, with your private vehicle (if it meets cantonal standards). Practice driving on Swiss roads before the exam.
Step 7: Pick up the converted driver's license If you pass both exams, the traffic office will issue the converted driver's license, valid in the Canton of Fribourg and throughout Switzerland. Verify that the data on the license is correct before leaving. The license will be valid according to Swiss federal regulations.
### Variable Times and Operational Support The overall duration depends on variable factors: processing times of the traffic office (which vary seasonally), availability of preparation courses, speed at which you complete the courses, availability of exam slots, and results of exam attempts. If you fail an exam, the time increases for a retake. Report your timing needs to the traffic office (e.g., if you need to drive for work as soon as possible) — sometimes it is possible to speed up the process.

## In brief - Security deposit: up to 3 months' rent in a blocked account - Rent dispute: within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Landlord's notice: cantonal form with 1/2/3 months' notice - Tenancy law: federal, identical in all cantons
## Key facts - **What**: Security deposit and tenant rights - Where: Canton of Fribourg (federal law CO art. 253 ff.) - Who: Tenants, landlords, cantonal conciliation authority - Amount: Up to 3 months' rent - Deadline: 30 days for conciliation appeal - Form: Notice only on official cantonal form - Competence: Swiss federal Code of Obligations
Tenancy law in Switzerland follows uniform federal rules codified in articles 253 and following of the Code of Obligations. In the canton of Fribourg, as in every Swiss canton, tenants and landlords operate under identical federal rules. This means that the rights of dispute, notice procedures, and management of the security deposit remain unchanged, regardless of the geographical region.
One of the most frequent issues concerns the security deposit. Federal law stipulates that the security deposit may not exceed three months' rent. It must be paid into a blocked bank account in the tenant's name only. The landlord may not use it except to offset certified amounts due or documented damages. If the deposit requested exceeds three months, the tenant has the right to contest it within specific deadlines.
A second critical aspect is the dispute of the initial rent. If the tenant believes the rent is excessive compared to local standards, they have 30 days to appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority for tenancy matters. This authority acts as the first instance of dispute resolution and can order a rent reduction if it finds a disproportion compared to local rents.
Notice represents another frequent area of conflict. The landlord can terminate the contract only by using the official cantonal form and respecting the notice periods: one month during the first year, two months from the second to the ninth year, and three months from the tenth year of occupancy. A notice drafted differently from the official form is null and void. ### Conciliation procedure in case of dispute
The cantonal conciliation authority in rental matters is the first competent body to resolve disputes between tenants and landlords. When a tenant disputes the initial rent, they have 30 days from receipt of the contract to file an appeal. The deadline is peremptory: after 30 days, the dispute is no longer admissible according to the Federal Code of Obligations. The conciliation authority examines whether the proposed rent complies with the parameters of reasonableness and conformity with the standards of the area. If the appeal is accepted, the authority can order a reduction in rent and reimbursement of the excess amounts already paid by the tenant.
The security deposit can also be disputed according to the same procedure. If the landlord requests a deposit exceeding three months' rent, the tenant can appeal to the conciliation authority within 30 days of the request. There are no appeal costs for the tenant; the procedure is simplified compared to an ordinary civil trial. The conciliation authority operates based on the Federal Code of Obligations, and its decisions can be appealed to the cantonal civil court within further established deadlines.
### The blocked account: protection of the tenant
The security deposit must be paid into a separate blocked bank account, solely in the tenant's name. This protection is fundamental: it prevents the landlord from accessing the funds for other purposes or using them as compensation for rents not yet due. During the lease, the money remains blocked. The landlord can only withdraw from the deposit if there are certified credits (documented outstanding rents or proven material damages) and must communicate in writing to the tenant the amount withdrawn, the reason, and the supporting documentation. At the end of the lease, the landlord has the obligation to return the deposit increased by the accrued interest, deducting only the legitimately due amounts. If the landlord unjustly withholds the return or does not comply with the return deadlines, the tenant can take legal action to obtain the amount plus moral damages.
### Termination: variable terms and nullity
The termination of the lease contract must be communicated in writing using exclusively the official cantonal form. No other form is legally accepted. An email, a personalized letter without the official form, or a verbal communication DOES NOT constitute a valid termination according to the Code of Obligations. The notice periods vary according to the seniority of the lease: one month for the first year, two months from the second to the ninth year, three months from the tenth year onwards. These terms are non-derogable and codified in federal law. A termination lacking the exact date, the original signature, or completed with the wrong form is null. The tenant can challenge it with the conciliation authority within 30 days of receipt and request the annulment of the termination.

On the first day of occupancy of a property, immediately check these essential aspects:
1. **Security deposit receipt**: Request a copy of the bank receipt confirming the deposit into a blocked account in your name. 2. Written contract: Keep a copy of the original contract with the date, landlord's signature, and all specific clauses. 3. Photographic attachments: Document the condition of the property with dated photos; immediately contest any pre-existing damages. 4. Meter readings: Record readings for electricity, gas, and water; request a written statement from the landlord. 5. Written communications: Keep all important communications in writing.
### Procedure for contesting rent
If the proposed rent seems excessive compared to the premises, property characteristics, and geographical area:
Day 1: Receive the contract and note the exact date of receipt. Days 2-30: Gather comparative data on similar rents in the area through online ads, local agencies, and cantonal databases. Days 25-30: Complete the appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority of Fribourg (form downloadable from the official website). Attach comparative documentation and state the reasons for the contestation. After the appeal: Wait for the summons to the conciliation office. It is not mandatory to be assisted by a lawyer. Decision: The authority communicates the outcome in writing within a period usually between 30 and 60 days. If favorable, the landlord is obliged to reduce the rent retroactively.
### Valid termination procedure
If the landlord communicates a termination:
1. Verify that the form is the official cantonal one (available at the Fribourg conciliation office). 2. Check the date of receipt, the original signature of the landlord, and the tenant's signature if required. 3. Calculate the notice period: first year = minimum 1 month; 2nd-9th year = 2 months; 10th year and beyond = 3 months from receipt. 4. If the termination does not comply with the form or federal terms, appeal to the conciliation authority within 30 days of receipt and request its annulment. 5. If the termination is correct, prepare to leave the property by the indicated date, possibly verifying the condition with the landlord.
Disputes over deposits, rents, and terminations are always first resolved by the cantonal conciliation authority of Fribourg. Only if dissatisfied with its verdict can one appeal to the cantonal civil court. Consult the official website of the Fribourg cantonal administration to find the competent office and download updated forms.

Tenancy law in the Canton of Fribourg is governed by the federal Code of Obligations (articles 253 and following), which establishes the same legal protections in every Swiss canton. Landlords and tenants must follow precise procedures for managing the security deposit, disputing the initial rent, and correctly executing the termination. Federal law protects both parties by ensuring transparency, clarity of rights, and access to rapid and free conciliation procedures.
### The security deposit: federal protection of the tenant
When a tenant signs a lease in the Canton of Fribourg, the landlord may require a security deposit to guarantee the payment of the last rents and to cover any damages. The Code of Obligations sets a precise limit: the deposit may not exceed three months' monthly rent. This maximum protects the tenant from excessive and abusive requests.
The deposit must be paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name. This block prevents the landlord from using the money before the end of the lease and provides legal guarantee of return. At the end of the lease, the deposit (with accrued interest) must be returned to the tenant within a reasonable time, except for documented deductions for legitimate damages or unpaid rents.

### Disputing the initial rent: the tenant's right
If a tenant believes that the initial rent is excessive or unjustified compared to the conditions of the property, federal law allows them to file a complaint. The dispute must be submitted within 30 days to the cantonal conciliation authority for tenancy matters in the Canton of Fribourg. This deadline is strict: if it expires, the rent is considered tacitly accepted.
The cantonal authority examines the complaint and verifies whether the rent is in accordance with market values and the characteristics of the leased property (size, condition, location, equipment). If the rent is found to be non-compliant, the authority may order the landlord to reduce it. This procedure is free or low-cost and does not require legal representation, making it an essential tool for protecting the right to housing. ### The notice of termination: forms, deadlines and legal validity
The termination of a lease agreement in the Canton of Fribourg must follow precise federal rules. The landlord wishing to terminate the contract is obliged to use the official cantonal form of Fribourg. This formality is mandatory: a notice of termination completed on a blank sheet, by email without the official document, or in any other format than the cantonal form is completely null and void and has no legal effect.
The notice of termination deadlines vary depending on the years of lease: - **First year of lease**: 1 month notice - Years 2-9 of lease: 2 months notice - From the tenth year of lease onwards: 3 months notice
These terms are set by federal law and apply regardless of what is written in the lease agreement. Clauses that provide for shorter deadlines are null; longer deadlines, however, remain valid if accepted in writing by both parties.
### How to obtain the official cantonal form of Fribourg
The official termination form for the Canton of Fribourg is available from the Fribourg cantonal administration. It can be downloaded from the official website of the Canton, obtained in paper format from the administrative offices, or by contacting the competent office by telephone to receive the updated document. Using the correct and current form is essential to ensure the legal validity of the notice of termination.
### Common errors in the termination procedure
Some terminations do not take effect because they are formally incorrect. The most frequent errors include: - Failure to use the official cantonal form (verbal termination or on personal paper) - Incorrect calculation of the notice period or the end date of the lease - Omission of data required by the form (tenant's name, address, landlord's data) - Failure to deliver the form to the recipient within the prescribed period (late delivery) - Absence of the landlord's handwritten signature on paper (if required by the cantonal procedure)
An invalid notice of termination has no legal effect, and the lease continues under the previous conditions. For this reason, it is always advisable to check with the cantonal conciliation authority whether the notice of termination has been correctly completed and notified before assuming that the lease has ended.

## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## The conciliation authority in rental matters
The Canton of Fribourg has a specialized conciliation authority for rental disputes. This cantonal administrative body plays a crucial role in resolving conflicts between tenants and landlords, serving as an accessible filter before resorting to lengthy and costly judicial proceedings. The authority is staffed by experts in rental law and is familiar with the specificities of the local real estate market.
### When to resort to the conciliation authority
The conciliation authority is competent for disputes related to: - Rental fees deemed excessive or unfair - Unjustified or incorrectly returned security deposits - Interpretation of ambiguous contractual clauses - Validity of a notice (e.g., notice on correct or incorrect form) - Liability for damage to the leased property (who pays, how much) - Maintenance and repair obligations of the property (landlord vs tenant responsibility) - Right of occupation after the end of the contract
### The conciliation procedure: operational steps
The procedure is simple and accessible even to those without legal experience. The tenant or landlord submits a written appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority within the prescribed deadline (usually 30 days from the occurrence of the disputed fact). In the appeal, the facts, reasons for the dispute, and what is requested (rent reduction, deposit return, declaration of notice nullity, etc.) are described.
The authority receives the appeal, communicates it to the counterparty, and summons them to a conciliation meeting. During the meeting, both parties present their positions, and the authority, based on experience and regulations, attempts to facilitate an amicable agreement. If an agreement is reached, it is binding and ends the dispute without the need for judicial recourse.
### If conciliation does not lead to an agreement
If no agreement is reached during the conciliation attempt, the authority drafts a technical report with its evaluations and conclusions. This report serves as a legal basis for any subsequent judicial appeal. Although not binding like a judgment, the authority's report has legal weight and facilitates subsequent resolution in court.
### Concrete advantages of the conciliation procedure
Resorting to the conciliation authority presents tangible advantages: - Free or minimal cost procedure (no court fees) - Short resolution times (usually weeks, not months) - Rental experts who evaluate disputes according to clear criteria - Amicable solution that preserves the relationship between the parties - Alternative to lengthy, costly, and conflictual court proceedings - Legal documentation recognized even for possible subsequent appeal
### How to contact the Fribourg conciliation authority
To initiate a conciliation procedure or obtain preliminary information, it is necessary to contact the Fribourg cantonal administration directly. Contact details, reception hours, and forms for submitting the appeal are available on the official website of the Canton of Fribourg. It is possible to submit the appeal in person at the counters, by mail, or sometimes through cantonal electronic platforms.
If you have doubts about your rights as tenants or landlords in the Canton of Fribourg, contacting the conciliation authority is the first recommended step.
